tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with README.md and CLAUDE.md to understand what this system does: manage IPTV channels, movies, and series, then feed them out to Home Assistant (YAML scripts) and Kodi (via JSON-RPC sync) and to any M3U-compatible player. README.md covers the stack, directory layout, and npm scripts, while CLAUDE.md is the authoritative, more detailed reference for framework wiring, server-function conventions, and the current database schema. Both agree on the same three-resource shape — channels, movies, series — that the rest of the tour builds on.

tour.title: Application Bootstrap & Routing
tour.description: router.tsx creates the TanStack Router instance, wires React Query's SSR integration so loader data hydrates cleanly on the client, and defines a custom search-param serializer so filter arrays (like `?countries=GR&countries=IR`) round-trip correctly. __root.tsx is the document shell: it renders the `<html>/<body>` scaffold, mounts the global navigation grouped by content type, and now includes a new 'Series Feed' link to `/series/m3u` alongside the existing Channels/Movies feed links. Together these two files are the only entry points TanStack Start requires — no app.tsx or ssr.tsx needed.
tour.languageLesson: TanStack Router's `Register` type must be declared with `interface`, not `type` — TypeScript's declaration merging (used here to attach the router type globally) only works on interfaces. This is a documented exception to the project's usual 'prefer type over interface' ESLint rule.

tour.title: Home & System Map
tour.description: The home page renders a system overview with highlight cards and per-section navigation for Live TV, Movies, and Series. Like __root.tsx, the Series section has just gained a 'Series Feed' card that links directly to `/series/m3u`, giving this page the same three-feed symmetry (Channels M3U/YAML, Movies M3U, Series M3U) you'll see formalized in the server routes later in the tour. Treat this page as a map: every card here corresponds to a route and server function you'll visit in upcoming steps.

tour.title: The Data Model
tour.description: schema.ts is the single source of truth for the database: a normalized `group_titles` lookup table shared by `channels`, `media`, and `series` via foreign key, so renaming a group's alias propagates everywhere it's used. `channels` holds live-TV rows with Kodi's `content_id`; `media` holds both movies and series episodes (distinguished by `media_type`, with `series_id` null for movies); `series` holds the grouping rows that episodes reference. This file has the highest fan-out in the whole codebase — nearly everything downstream, from Zod validators to server queries to forms, is generated from or references these table definitions.
tour.languageLesson: Drizzle ORM defines tables as plain TypeScript objects and derives row types via `typeof table.$inferSelect`, so the schema file is both the runtime table definition and the compile-time type source — there's no separate interface to keep in sync.

tour.title: DB Client & Validation
tour.description: src/db/index.ts wraps the Drizzle client in a Proxy that lazily connects on first property access — this is what lets server-only code import `db` without breaking client-side bundling during SSR. src/db/validators.ts holds the Zod schemas (channel/media/series create + update) that every form and server function validates against, plus the ISO 3166-1 country-code list used for channel filtering. Both files sit directly on top of schema.ts from the previous step: validators.ts imports the table shapes, and index.ts re-exports them as one convenient barrel.
tour.languageLesson: The Proxy pattern here intercepts property access (`get` trap) to defer `initDb()` until the first real use, avoiding a top-level side effect that would otherwise run during module import — a common trick for isomorphic code that must not touch a database connection on the client.

tour.title: The Shared Server Engine
tour.description: shared.ts has the highest fan-in of any file in the project (13 incoming references) — it's the generic engine that channels.ts, movies.ts, and series.ts all build on. It centralizes paginated list queries, get-by-id, search, toggle-active, create/update logic, and the group-title upsert (resolving a string like 'US| ENTERTAINMENT' to a `group_titles` foreign key). Rather than duplicating CRUD logic three times for three resource types, each resource-specific file is a thin wrapper that calls into this shared layer with different table/schema parameters.
tour.languageLesson: This is a parameterized-engine pattern: rather than TypeScript generics over the table type, the functions here take the Drizzle table object as a runtime parameter and rely on Drizzle's own type inference to keep each call site type-safe — a pragmatic middle ground when full generic typing over ORM tables gets unwieldy.

tour.title: Server Functions & API Routes
tour.description: channels.ts and movies.ts are barrels that re-export CRUD, export, and sync wrappers built on shared.ts. series.ts goes further: it now exposes a standalone `getActiveSeriesM3u()` function that groups active series by the series' own custom name (not the group-titles lookup), and that same function is called from two places — the `exportActiveSeriesM3u` createServerFn used by the UI, and a brand-new `GET /series/m3u` route in server.ts. server.ts is the custom Nitro entry that intercepts `/channels/m3u`, `/channels/yaml`, `/movies/m3u`, `/series/m3u`, and `/play/:table/:id` ahead of the default SSR handler, building M3U/YAML responses directly — the project now exposes three parallel direct-feed URLs (channels, movies, series) plus the Home Assistant YAML feed, all before falling through to page rendering.

tour.title: The Channels Page
tour.description: channels.index.tsx is the highest-fan-out route in the app: it composes the reusable ListStream table, several shadcn/ui primitives, and server functions from channels.ts and shared.ts into a fully server-filtered, paginated channel list with Export M3U/YAML and Sync Kodi actions. ListStream.tsx itself is reused across the Channels, Movies, and Series pages — the same table renders three different resource types by taking column/action config as props. ActiveSwitch.tsx wires each row's active toggle to an optimistic React Query mutation via `setQueriesData`, so the UI updates instantly before the server confirms.

tour.title: Forms & Validation
tour.description: ChannelForm.tsx and SeriesForm.tsx are the create/edit forms bound to the Zod schemas from validators.ts (Step 5). ChannelForm resolves the group-title and country-code fields against schema.ts and calls into channels.ts on submit; SeriesForm is more involved, managing dynamic episode rows that each reference a movie via MovieCombobox, plus season/episode numbers, and it calls the standalone series.ts server functions directly. Both forms show the same end-to-end path: UI form -> Zod validation -> server function -> shared.ts engine -> database.

tour.title: M3U Pipeline
tour.description: m3u-parser.ts is the ingestion side: it tokenizes `#EXTINF` lines from an imported M3U file and classifies each entry as a channel or media item, extracting series base name, season/episode, and year along the way. m3u-export.ts is the output side: `generateM3u` formats active DB rows back into M3U playlist text, preferring a country-derived group title over the raw group_titles value. server/m3u.ts wraps `generateM3u` as the createServerFn behind `/channels/m3u` and `/movies/m3u`, while the parallel `/series/m3u` route from Step 7 reuses the same `generateM3u` formatter through series.ts's `getActiveSeriesM3u` — one export function, three feeds.

tour.title: Home Assistant YAML Export
tour.description: yaml-export.ts generates a plain top-level YAML mapping of scripts — deliberately without a `script:` wrapper key — because the output file is consumed via `script: !include channels.yaml` in a Home Assistant configuration. Only channels with both a `scriptAlias` and a Kodi-synced `contentId` are included; an empty result is `{}` rather than null so the `!include` still yields a valid mapping. server/yaml.ts wraps this as `getActiveChannelsYaml`, which server.ts's `/channels/yaml` route calls only after running a Kodi sync first — serving a 502 if that sync fails, to avoid publishing stale content IDs.
tour.languageLesson: YAML's `!include` directive (a Home Assistant-specific tag) expects the included file's top level to already be the right shape for its context — hence generating a bare mapping instead of nesting it under a `script:` key, which would double-wrap it when included under an existing `script:` block.

tour.title: Kodi Sync Integration
tour.description: runKodiSync (kodi.ts) calls Kodi's JSON-RPC `PVR.GetChannels` method and updates only the `content_id` column on matching channel rows — nothing else. The actual matching logic lives in the pure, independently-testable `matchKodiChannels` in kodi-url.ts: it tries the channel's `name` field before `tvgName` against Kodi's `label`, case- and whitespace-insensitively, because Kodi labels are CMS display names ('CNN') while the raw M3U `tvgName` is often something like 'US| CNN FHD'. The companion `resolveKodiConnection` helper builds the JSON-RPC endpoint URL and optional HTTP Basic auth header from `KODI_URL`/`KODI_HOST`/`KODI_PORT`/`KODI_USER`/`KODI_PASSWORD` env vars, which must be set in both dev and prod env profiles.

tour.title: Shared UI Package
tour.description: The @iptvchannels/ui workspace package supplies the shadcn/ui component layer every route and form in this app builds on. utils.ts's `cn()` helper — merging Tailwind classes via clsx + tailwind-merge — has the highest fan-in of any UI-layer file, since virtually every styled component calls it. button.tsx (built on class-variance-authority) and select.tsx (a ten-part composite over Radix Select) show the two dominant shadcn patterns you'll see repeated across the package: variant-driven primitives and multi-part composites.
tour.languageLesson: class-variance-authority (cva) defines component style variants as a typed config object, then `cn()` merges the resulting class string with any caller-supplied `className` — Tailwind-merge resolves conflicting utility classes (e.g. two different `px-*` values) by keeping the last one, which is what lets consumers safely override styles.

tour.title: Database Scripts & Migrations
tour.description: seed-channels.sh imports channels from an M3U file using a staging-table-plus-COPY pattern for bulk-insert speed, then joins against group_titles by FK. The 0001_elite_naoko.sql migration is where the normalized group_titles lookup, plus the media and series tables, were introduced with foreign keys back to it — the schema.ts model from Step 4 made physical. drizzle.config.ts ties it all together with an env-driven `schemaFilter` that targets either the shared `iptvchannels` Postgres schema locally or `public` in backward-compatible environments.
tour.languageLesson: SQL migrations should be idempotent and strictly ordered — Drizzle Kit tracks applied migrations in a journal file (`_journal.json`) so `db:migrate` only ever runs forward, never re-applying a migration that's already landed.
